407.title: Bold outside, careful inside
407.hook: be confident about outside things and cautious about your own judgments (Discourses 2.1)
407.howItsDone: Stoic readers often use this chapter to sort their fears, acting boldly on outside things they've been avoiding while slowing down their own quick judgments.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was stand firm. Your line was let the branches move in the wind, while the roots stay where they are.

Hunters in the ancient world had a clever trick for catching deer. They'd string a line of feathers across the woods. The feathers fluttered, the deer panicked and ran the other way, straight into the nets the hunters had set. The deer weren't cowards. They were afraid of the wrong thing, and fearless about the wrong thing. Epictetus thought most of us live exactly like those deer.
screen: `A LINE OF FEATHERS.` → `THE DEER RUN INTO THE NETS.` → `AFRAID OF THE WRONG THING.`

segments.voice: Book two of the Discourses opens with chapter one: that confidence isn't at odds with caution. The Stoics claimed you should be both, completely bold and completely careful, and people thought that sounded like nonsense. Epictetus explains. Be careful where the real danger is: in your own will. That's where you can actually go wrong, by agreeing too fast, wanting the wrong thing, acting on a bad impression. And be bold about everything outside the will, because nothing out there can make you bad. Then he shows how we flip it. We're terrified of things outside us, death, exile, pain, losing face, and reckless inside, quick to agree with any thought that comes along. Like the deer, fleeing the feathers into the nets. He has another image for the outside fears. Death and pain, he says, are like the masks that scare little children. Turn the mask around and look at the back. It doesn't bite. What frightens us is mostly our opinion about death and pain, not the things themselves. This doesn't mean being careless with your health or safety; Epictetus would still have you look both ways crossing the street. It means putting your carefulness where it does the most good, on your own judgments, and letting your courage go out into the world.

segments.voice: Think of one outside thing you've been avoiding out of fear, a phone call, a conversation, speaking up, and turn it around like a mask: what's actually on the back? Usually it's discomfort, not disaster. Then turn inward to one judgment you made too fast, and hold both: bold out there, careful in here.
Bold outside. Epictetus' answer to the Stoic paradox: be confident about what's outside your will, and save your caution for your own judgments.
Your line: turn the mask around. The back of it doesn't bite. That's day four hundred seven.

408.title: Play the ball well
408.hook: players care about handling the ball well, not about the ball (Discourses 2.5)
408.carry: let the ball be the ball
408.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners separate the outcome of a task from the way they do it, and judge their day by the quality of their effort, the way the ball players in this chapter care only about the throwing and catching.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was bold outside: confident about outside things, careful with your own judgments. Your line was turn the mask around.

Watch a pickup basketball game in a park. Nobody stops to argue about whether the ball is a good ball or a bad ball. It's just the ball. Everything they care about is what they do with it: the pass, the catch, the footwork, the shot. A great player with a scuffed, half-flat ball is still a joy to watch. Epictetus used ball games, and dice, to answer a hard puzzle in Stoic thought.
screen: `NOBODY ARGUES ABOUT THE BALL.` → `THE PASS, THE CATCH, THE SHOT.` → `A HARD STOIC PUZZLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the puzzle. The Stoics said outside things, money, health, even life itself, are neither good nor bad; only how we use them is. So why care about anything? Why not shrug at everything? That's Discourses book two, chapter five: how greatness of mind fits with carefulness. Epictetus answers with games. Look at people playing dice, he says. The dice and the counters don't matter, and you can't control what falls. But using well what falls is your job, and you can do it with real care. Then the ball players. None of them argues about whether the ball is good or bad. They argue about throwing and catching, and there they're all skill, speed and attention. Then a game with far more at stake. Socrates, he says, knew how to play ball, even in the court where he was tried. And what was the ball? Life. Chains. Exile. Drinking poison. Being taken from his wife, and leaving his children without a father. Those were what he was handed, and he handled them with good form. So: don't treat the ball as everything, and don't treat the game as nothing. Pour all your care into the playing. A job, a diagnosis, a family situation: those are what's been tossed to you. How you catch them and pass them on is where the skill lives.

segments.voice: Think of one task waiting for you today, ordinary or hard, and notice what you're hoping it gets you: praise, a result, a relief. That's the ball; set it down for now. Then picture doing the task itself with full care, the first step, the attention, the craft of it, and feel the difference between playing for the prize and playing well.
Sphaira. Greek for ball: Epictetus' image for life's outside things, the dice and the ball we're handed, where the point isn't the ball but how we play it.
Your line: let the ball be the ball. The care goes into the play. Until tomorrow.

409.title: Who am I here?
409.hook: remember who you are, a human, a citizen, a son, a brother, and act from each (Discourses 2.10)
409.carry: each name tells you what to do
409.howItsDone: Some Stoic readers pause before entering a room or conversation to name the role they're stepping into, and ask what it asks of them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sphaira, the ball Socrates played with good form. Your line was let the ball be the ball.

In a single afternoon you might be a manager in a meeting, a customer on hold, a daughter on the phone with her mother, a neighbor waving across the fence, and a stranger letting someone merge in traffic. Each one asks something slightly different of you. It's easy to switch without noticing, and sometimes to bring the wrong one into the room: the boss into the family dinner, the tired customer into a talk with a friend. Epictetus had a method for this.
screen: `MANAGER, CUSTOMER, DAUGHTER, NEIGHBOR.` → `EACH ASKS SOMETHING DIFFERENT.` → `THE WRONG ONE IN THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book two, chapter ten: how to find what you owe from the names you carry. Consider who you are, Epictetus says. First, a human being, which means someone with a will, and nothing in you ranks higher than that. Second, a citizen of the world, a part of it, and not a minor part. So act the way a hand or a foot would act if it could think: never just for itself, always as part of the whole body. Then the names come closer to home. Remember you're a son. That name asks you to treat what's yours as your father's, to give way to him, never to speak badly of him to others. Remember you're a brother: yield, be courteous, and never fight your brother over things that don't really matter. If you sit on a city council, remember you're a councilor. If young, young; if old, old; if a father, a father. Each name, if you stop and think about it, tells you what to do. His examples are sons, brothers and fathers. The method fits daughters, sisters, parents, partners, coworkers, anyone. And it's simple enough to use at a doorway: which name am I carrying into this room, and what does it ask of me?

410.title: Start with weakness
410.hook: philosophy begins with noticing your own weakness (Discourses 2.11)
410.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism begin by naming an area where they feel certain but may be wrong, and treat that honest admission as the start of their training.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was onoma: each name you carry tells you what you owe. Your line was each name tells you what to do.

Nobody walks into a calculus class insisting they already know calculus. Nobody sits down at a piano for the first time convinced they can play Chopin. With those things, we know what we don't know. But ask a room full of people what's fair, what a good life is, or how to treat a difficult relative, and plenty of people are sure they already know. Epictetus found that strange, and said it's exactly where philosophy has to begin.
screen: `NOBODY THINKS THEY KNOW CALCULUS.` → `EVERYONE KNOWS WHAT'S FAIR.` → `WHERE PHILOSOPHY BEGINS.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book two, chapter eleven: what the beginning of philosophy is. For anyone who comes in by the right door, Epictetus says, it begins with noticing your own weakness and inability in the things that matter most. Why there? Nobody is born with an idea of a right triangle, or of a musical interval. We learn those from teachers, so nobody who hasn't learned them thinks they know them. But good and bad, fair and unfair, noble and shameful: everyone arrives with some sense of those. We're born with the outline, and because we have it, we assume we know how to fill it in. That's the trap. Two people can both love justice and still disagree completely about what's just in a given case. You can't both be right, and seeming right to yourself isn't enough; people who are wrong feel just as certain. So philosophy starts by admitting that, and then looks for a standard, the way people found the balance for weighing and the rule for measuring straight lines, so that arguments could be settled by something outside our feelings. It's an oddly hopeful beginning. Weakness here doesn't mean you're bad. It means you're honest about being unfinished. The person who says, I don't actually know how to handle my anger, is further along than the person who's sure they've got it figured out.
screen: `THE RIGHT DOOR IN.` · `NO ONE IS BORN KNOWING GEOMETRY.` · `WE ALL THINK WE KNOW WHAT'S GOOD.` · `LOOK FOR A STANDARD.` · then, large: `START WITH WEAKNESS.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself, gently: where am I sure I'm right, and might not be? Let one come up, about a person, a decision, a way of doing things, and say plainly inside: here, I'm not as strong as I think. Notice whether that feels uncomfortable or like a strange relief, and let the admission be a beginning.
Astheneia. Greek for weakness: Epictetus' door into philosophy, noticing that in the things that matter most, we're less sure and less able than we think.
Your line: honest about being unfinished. That's the right door into philosophy. See you tomorrow.

411.title: Without the crowd
411.hook: the singer is only anxious when he wants the crowd's applause (Discourses 2.13)
411.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners often meet nerves by asking what they want that isn't in their control, usually approval, and turning their attention back to doing the task well.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was astheneia, the weakness that opens the door to philosophy. Your line was honest about being unfinished.

In the shower, a person can sing. Really sing. Full voice, the high note, the whole song. Then someone hands that same person a microphone at a wedding, and the throat closes up. The voice didn't change between the bathroom and the reception hall. Neither did the skill. Something else walked into the room. Epictetus describes this exact moment, with a singer in a theater, and he names what walked in.
screen: `IN THE SHOWER, YOU CAN SING.` → `A MICROPHONE AT A WEDDING.` → `SOMETHING ELSE WALKED IN.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book two, chapter thirteen, on anxiety. Epictetus starts like a doctor making a diagnosis. When I see someone anxious, he says, I ask: what does this person want? If they didn't want something outside their control, why would they be anxious? Then the musician. A lyre player singing by himself isn't anxious at all. But when he walks into the theater, even with a fine voice and beautiful playing, he is. Why? Because he doesn't only want to sing well. He wants to be applauded, and that isn't up to him. Where his skill is, there's confidence. Bring in a crowd he wants something from, and the anxiety arrives. Then a pair of real people. When Zeno, the founder of the Stoic school, went to see King Antigonus, Zeno wasn't anxious. Antigonus was. The king wanted to impress the philosopher; the philosopher wanted nothing from the king. The one with the power was the one sweating. The fix isn't to stop caring about doing well. Practice your craft, Epictetus says; get good. The fix is to notice when part of you is singing for the applause, and bring your attention back to the singing. You can stand in a full room and still, inside, be singing without the crowd.

412.title: Habits grow by use
412.hook: walk to become a walker, read to become a reader (Discourses 2.18)
412.carry: one ordinary step at a time
412.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners often pick one small virtue to practice repeatedly, on the principle that each act strengthens the habit, and replace an unwanted habit with a chosen one.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was agōnia: the singer alone is calm, and the anxiety comes with wanting applause. Your line was singing for the applause.

After a week in bed with the flu, you get up and try to walk to the mailbox. Your legs feel like someone else's. A week ago you didn't think about walking at all; now it takes effort. Nothing was injured. You just didn't use them, and they quietly got weaker. Epictetus used almost exactly that example, a person getting out of bed after ten days, to explain how everything in us grows or shrinks.
screen: `A WEEK IN BED WITH THE FLU.` → `LEGS LIKE SOMEONE ELSE'S.` → `NOTHING INJURED, JUST UNUSED.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book two, chapter eighteen. Every habit and every ability, Epictetus says, is kept up and made stronger by the actions that match it. Walking by walking. Running by running. Want to be a good reader? Read. A writer? Write. Stop reading for thirty days and do something else instead, and you'll see what happens. Lie in bed for ten days, then try a long walk, and you'll see how weak your legs have become. So here's his rule, as plain as anything in the Discourses. If you want to be able to do something, make a habit of doing it. If you don't want to do something, don't do it, and get used to doing something else in its place. Notice that second half. He doesn't just say stop. He says replace. A habit leaves a space, and something will fill it. Then he turns from the body to the mind, which for him is the whole point. Patience, honesty, gentleness, courage work the same way. Each kind act makes the next one easier. Each honest answer makes honesty more natural. And the other direction too: every time you give in to a bad reaction, you haven't just had one bad moment; you've strengthened the habit. Nobody becomes patient by reading about patience. You become patient the way you become a walker: one ordinary step at a time.
screen: `WALKING BY WALKING.` · `TEN DAYS IN BED, WEAK LEGS.` · `DON'T JUST STOP: REPLACE.` · `PATIENCE GROWS THE SAME WAY.` · then, large: `HABITS GROW BY USE.`

Picture doing it once, then again tomorrow, and the day after, and feel how the second time is a little easier than the first.

413.title: Count the calm days
413.hook: count the days you weren't angry: every day, then every other, then every third (Discourses 2.18)
413.carry: give the anger nothing to burn
413.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism keep a private tally of days without anger, expecting setbacks and watching the gaps between angry days grow.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hexis: habits grow by use. Your line was one ordinary step at a time. Today ends the week.

Days on a language app. Days on this path. Steps on a watch. Streaks are everywhere, and a number going up has a way of keeping people showing up. Miss a day, and it stings a little. The idea is older than it looks. Epictetus gave his students a streak to keep, not for steps or lessons, but for something much harder: the days they got through without losing their temper.
screen: `STREAKS EVERYWHERE.` → `A NUMBER GOING UP.` → `DAYS WITHOUT LOSING YOUR TEMPER.`

segments.voice: It's the same chapter as yesterday, Discourses book two, chapter eighteen, where hexis is formed. If you don't want to be quick-tempered, Epictetus says, then don't feed the habit. Give it nothing that makes it grow. And at first, keep quiet, and count the days you weren't angry. I used to be angry every day. Now every other day. Then every third. Then every fourth. And if you go thirty days, he says, make an offering to God, because the habit is first weakened, and then wiped out. Notice how kind this is. He doesn't say, never get angry again, starting today. He expects relapses. He's measuring the gaps between angry days getting longer. In the same chapter he gives a tool for the moment anger rises. When an impression hits you hard, don't let it carry you off. Say to it: wait for me a little, impression. Let me see what you are, and what you're about. Let me test you. That little pause is how the count goes up. And his very first instruction is easy to miss: keep quiet. Be still at first, and give the anger nothing to burn. The counting grows out of that stillness. The week in a breath: bold outside, sphaira, onoma, astheneia, agōnia, habits grow by use, and now count the calm days.
screen: `DON'T FEED THE HABIT.` · `EVERY DAY, EVERY OTHER, EVERY THIRD.` · `WAIT FOR ME A LITTLE, IMPRESSION.` · `KEEP STILL, THEN COUNT.` · then, large: `COUNT THE CALM DAYS.`

segments.voice: Think back over today, or yesterday if today has barely started, and notice any anger in it, a flash, a slow burn, a sharp word, without judging. If the day was calm, let that be one quiet mark on the count; if it wasn't, no scolding. Then rehearse the pause: picture a hot moment, and hear yourself say, wait a little, let me see what you are.
Orgē. Greek for anger: Epictetus' plan for a quick temper, angry every day, then every other, then every third, until thirty calm days in a row.
Your line: give the anger nothing to burn. Every other day is progress too. Another week, done.
